Safe Administration of Medication Policy

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how Alderbridge Care Group ensures medication is prescribed, ordered, stored, administered, recorded and reviewed safely and consistently across every site. It applies to every member of staff who has any contact with medication, from a registered nurse administering an injection to a housekeeping colleague who happens to find a dropped tablet on the floor. It does not cover community support workers assisting a person to self-administer under a documented capacity assessment — that specific activity is governed by the Self-Administration of Medication Policy, which this policy defers to entirely rather than duplicating.

Policy statement

Alderbridge Care Group believes that safe medication practice is one of the clearest, most measurable expressions of good care. Errors are treated as a system-level learning opportunity in the first instance, not automatically as individual misconduct, in line with the Medication Error Report Form's own no-blame first-response principle — although a pattern of repeated, avoidable error, or a single deliberately concealed error, is escalated through the Disciplinary Procedure.

Definitions

**MAR chart** the Medication Administration Record on which every dose given, refused, or omitted is signed for at the time of administration, never in advance and never retrospectively without a documented late-entry reason. **PRN medication** medication prescribed to be given only when required, subject to its own written PRN protocol describing the specific circumstances, maximum frequency and maximum daily dose. **Homely remedy** a limited over-the-counter remedy that may be given without an individual prescription, governed separately by the Homely Remedies Policy. **Competency assessment** the observed, signed-off assessment confirming a named member of staff is safe to administer medication unsupervised, distinct from simply having attended training. **Controlled drug** a medication subject to the additional legal controls and double-signing requirements set out separately in the Controlled Drugs Procedure.

Governance and reporting structure

Medication safety sits within the wider clinical governance structure chaired by the Alderbridge Quality Lead, who reports directly to the Chief Executive and, in aggregate and anonymised form, to the Board twice a year. Each site's registered manager attends a monthly medication safety huddle, initially trialled at Riverside House and rolled out to all sites in 2025, at which the previous month's MAR completion percentage, any Medication Error Report Form raised, and any near miss are reviewed as a standing agenda item rather than only when a problem has already occurred. A site whose monthly huddle identifies a recurring theme (for example, repeated late administration around a particular shift handover time) is expected to propose its own local corrective action rather than wait for a instruction from Central Support Office, though the Quality Lead remains available to support that local work.

Worked example

A worked example illustrates how the six rights and the exceptions above interact in practice. A resident at Moorland View is prescribed a routine morning tablet at 08:00. At 07:55 the senior carer finds the resident asleep. Rather than waking the resident immediately, the carer completes the rest of the round first and returns at 08:20, within the reasonable delay this policy allows for a non-time-critical medication, and administers the dose then, recording the actual time given and noting the short delay as a timing variance rather than treating it as an omission. Later the same morning, the same resident is due a second, genuinely time-critical medication at 12:00 which must be given within a 30-minute window either side under its own prescriber instruction; on that occasion the carer would instead wake the resident gently within the window, because the reasonable-delay allowance in this policy applies to routine, not time-critical, medication, and the two should never be treated the same way by a member of staff under time pressure.

Ordering and supply

Medication is ordered from the resident's usual community pharmacy in line with the Medication Ordering and Stock Policy's timescales, with a named member of staff at each site responsible for reconciling what arrives against what was ordered before it is placed into stock. A discrepancy between the pharmacy delivery note and the physical delivery is queried with the pharmacy the same day, never assumed to be a simple counting error.

Storage

Medication is stored in the locked medication trolley or cupboard specified for the site, with the trolley locked and the key on the person of the administering staff member at all times during a round, never left in the lock. Incident Reporting Policy

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how every accident, incident, near miss, medication error and property damage event
is reported, investigated and learned from at Alderbridge Care Group. It applies to every site and every
person present — staff, people supported, visitors and contractors.

Policy statement

Alderbridge treats thorough incident reporting as one of its most important safety tools, and actively
encourages reporting even where an event seems minor, since a genuine safety culture depends on
seeing the full picture, not only the events serious enough to be impossible to overlook.

Definitions

**Incident** any unplanned event that caused or could have caused harm or damage. **Near miss** an
event that could have caused harm but did not, on this occasion. **RIDDOR-reportable incident** an
incident meeting the specific statutory threshold requiring notification to the Health and Safety Executive.
**Root cause** the underlying, systemic reason an incident occurred, as distinct from its immediate,
surface-level cause.

Roles and responsibilities

**Any member of staff** witnessing or discovering an incident reports it the same shift using the
appropriate form. **The registered manager** reviews every incident at their site, escalating a
RIDDOR-reportable or otherwise serious incident to the Health and Safety Lead immediately. **The Health
and Safety Lead** coordinates cross-site trend analysis and reports to the quarterly Health and Safety
Committee.

1. Report every accident, incident and near miss using the appropriate form (the Accident and Incident
Report Form, Safeguarding Referral Form, or Medication Error Report Form as applicable) within 24
hours, regardless of how minor it seems.

2. Take any immediate action needed to make the situation safe before completing the paperwork, since
first aid and safety always come before documentation.

3. The registered manager reviews every report the same or next working day, identifying whether any
immediate further action is needed.

Medication reconciliation on admission and transfer

Every resident's full medication list is reconciled against the prescribing GP's own record at admission, and again at any hospital transfer in either direction, since a mismatch between what a resident is believed to be taking and what they are actually prescribed is one of the most common sources of a serious medication error. Post-incident review process

Following any Tier 2 or higher incident, IT leads a post-incident review within 10 working days of resolution, documenting what worked, what did not, and any change needed to this plan, the severity model, or a specific system's own resilience.

Detailed containment procedure by system type

Containment differs meaningfully depending on the affected system's nature. For a single endpoint device (a laptop, tablet or desktop), IT disconnects it from the network immediately, either physically or via remote network access revocation, without powering it off, since powering off can destroy volatile memory evidence useful to a later forensic review. For a server-based system, IT isolates the affected server segment at the network switch level rather than the individual server, since a compromised server may have already spread laterally to a degree not yet visible. For a cloud-hosted system, IT contacts the cloud provider's own security team in parallel with internal containment, since a cloud environment's containment options differ from an on-premises one and often require provider-side action IT cannot take unilaterally.

Detailed containment procedure by system type (continued)

For a network device itself (a router, switch or firewall), IT does not simply power-cycle it, since this can both destroy evidence and, in some compromise scenarios, trigger a malicious payload configured to activate on restart; instead, a specialist is engaged to assess before any restart is attempted. For a shared care records system spanning multiple sites, IT considers whether a partial, site-by-site isolation is sufficient rather than isolating the entire system nationally, weighing the containment benefit against the operational disruption a full isolation would cause to sites with no evidence of compromise.

Evidence preservation

Before any remediation step that could alter or destroy evidence, IT takes a forensic image or detailed log export of the affected system where practicable, since a later insurance claim, regulatory enquiry, or law enforcement investigation may depend on evidence that a hurried remediation step could otherwise destroy. This preservation step does not delay an urgent containment action itself, but is completed as soon as the immediate containment is achieved and before full remediation begins.

Appendix: the two-stage test explained

This appendix explains the Act's own two-stage test in more practical detail. Stage one asks whether the person has an impairment or disturbance of the mind or brain, whether permanent or temporary — this alone does not determine incapacity, only whether the second stage needs to be considered at all. Stage two asks whether that impairment means the person cannot, at the time the decision needs to be made, understand relevant information about the decision, retain that information long enough to use it, weigh it up as part of the decision-making process, or communicate their decision by any means. A person lacks capacity for the specific decision only if stage one applies and they fail any one part of stage two — both stages genuinely matter, and staff are trained not to skip from 'has a diagnosis' straight to 'lacks capacity' without properly working through stage two.

When a decision genuinely cannot wait

For a decision that must be made urgently and there is no attorney or existing best interests decision in place, the treating professional or care team makes the decision in the person's best interests using the information available at that moment, records the reasoning fully as soon as practicable afterward, and reviews it with fuller information once the urgency has passed, since acting reasonably with incomplete information in a genuine emergency is preferable to delaying necessary care while a more complete process is followed.

Following any Tier 2 or higher incident, IT leads a post-incident review within 10 working days of resolution, documenting what worked, what did not, and any change needed to this plan, the severity model, or a specific system's own resilience.

Detailed containment procedure by system type

Containment differs meaningfully depending on the affected system's nature. For a single endpoint device (a laptop, tablet or desktop), IT disconnects it from the network immediately, either physically or via remote network access revocation, without powering it off, since powering off can destroy volatile memory evidence useful to a later forensic review. For a server-based system, IT isolates the affected server segment at the network switch level rather than the individual server, since a compromised server may have already spread laterally to a degree not yet visible. For a cloud-hosted system, IT contacts the cloud provider's own security team in parallel with internal containment, since a cloud environment's containment options differ from an on-premises one and often require provider-side action IT cannot take unilaterally.

Detailed containment procedure by system type (continued)

For a network device itself (a router, switch or firewall), IT does not simply power-cycle it, since this can both destroy evidence and, in some compromise scenarios, trigger a malicious payload configured to activate on restart; instead, a specialist is engaged to assess before any restart is attempted. For a shared care records system spanning multiple sites, IT considers whether a partial, site-by-site isolation is sufficient rather than isolating the entire system nationally, weighing the containment benefit against the operational disruption a full isolation would cause to sites with no evidence of compromise.

Before any remediation step that could alter or destroy evidence, IT takes a forensic image or detailed log export of the affected system where practicable, since a later insurance claim, regulatory enquiry, or law enforcement investigation may depend on evidence that a hurried remediation step could otherwise destroy. This preservation step does not delay an urgent containment action itself, but is completed as soon as the immediate containment is achieved and before full remediation begins.

Following any Tier 2 or higher incident, IT leads a post-incident review within 10 working days of resolution, documenting what worked, what did not, and any change needed to this plan, the severity model, or a specific system's own resilience.

Detailed containment procedure by system type

Containment differs meaningfully depending on the affected system's nature. For a single endpoint device (a laptop, tablet or desktop), IT disconnects it from the network immediately, either physically or via remote network access revocation, without powering it off, since powering off can destroy volatile memory evidence useful to a later forensic review. For a server-based system, IT isolates the affected server segment at the network switch level rather than the individual server, since a compromised server may have already spread laterally to a degree not yet visible. For a cloud-hosted system, IT contacts the cloud provider's own security team in parallel with internal containment, since a cloud environment's containment options differ from an on-premises one and often require provider-side action IT cannot take unilaterally.

Detailed containment procedure by system type (continued)

For a network device itself (a router, switch or firewall), IT does not simply power-cycle it, since this can both destroy evidence and, in some compromise scenarios, trigger a malicious payload configured to activate on restart; instead, a specialist is engaged to assess before any restart is attempted. For a shared care records system spanning multiple sites, IT considers whether a partial, site-by-site isolation is sufficient rather than isolating the entire system nationally, weighing the containment benefit against the operational disruption a full isolation would cause to sites with no evidence of compromise.

Before any remediation step that could alter or destroy evidence, IT takes a forensic image or detailed log export of the affected system where practicable, since a later insurance claim, regulatory enquiry, or law enforcement investigation may depend on evidence that a hurried remediation step could otherwise destroy. This preservation step does not delay an urgent containment action itself, but is completed as soon as the immediate containment is achieved and before full remediation begins.
